<translation>
<pb n="116"/>he does not dedicate <note>merits</note> for the sake of resources and so forth. Thus, the dedications of merits such as generosity become concordant causes, and so that Tathagata possesses <term>inexhaustible merit</term>; by that, he acts for the sake of beings forever. Because all the roots of virtue of the Tathagata are also never exhausted in the sphere of Nirvana without remainder, for that reason his roots of virtue never go to waste. For that very reason, the bodies of the Tathagatas are called <term>permanent</term>. This is because the previously assembled body of the Noble One <note>the form body</note>, through the power of previous momentum, continues without effort for as long as cyclic existence lasts, like a wish-fulfilling jewel. Thus, the Tathagata is said to have "roots of virtue that never waste away," which result in the welfare of beings.

"Adorned with patience; the basis of the treasures of merit; graced by the minor marks; flowering with the major marks; suitable and harmonious in conduct; and nothing about him is discordant to behold" — these six phrases show which body the Blessed One uses to perform which benefit for beings. That body is the <term>Form Body</term> <gloss>Rupakaya</gloss>. The perfection of that Form Body is also shown through five aspects: perfection of the primary cause, perfection of the distinct causes, perfection of essence, perfection of state, and perfection of activity.

In that regard, "adorned with patience" shows the perfection of the primary cause. Patience is the cause of beauty, as it is said: "Through patience, one becomes beautiful." Furthermore, it is said: "This is the path that leads to an ugly complexion: namely, anger and malice." Thus, patience is explained as the cause of beauty because it maintains its own nature and completely abandons its opposite side <note>anger</note>. 

"The basis of the treasures of merit" shows the perfection of the distinct causes. The causes for the individual parts of the body are the distinct causes. This should be understood from the teaching on the inexhaustible collection of merit within the teaching on inexhaustible <pb n="117"/> diligence in the <term>Noble Inexhaustible Intelligence Sūtra</term> <gloss>Arya-Akshayamati-paripriccha</gloss>. There it is said that from ten times the mass of merit of all sentient beings, one single hair-pore of the Tathagata is accomplished. From eight times the mass of merit required to accomplish all the hair-pores, one minor mark is accomplished. From a thousand times the mass of merit involved in accomplishing all the minor marks, each major mark is fully accomplished, except for the hair-treasure <note>the urna between the brows</note>, the crown-protrusion <note>ushnisha</note>, and the conch-like dharma-throat. From ten thousand times the mass of merit involved in accomplishing the twenty-nine marks, the hair-treasure is accomplished. From a hundred thousand times the mass of merit involved in accomplishing the hair-treasure, the crown-protrusion is accomplished. From a hundred billion times the mass of merit involved in accomplishing the crown-protrusion, the conch-like dharma-throat of the Tathagata is accomplished. Thus, that Form Body of the Tathagata is the basis of the treasures of merit.

"Graced by the minor marks" and "flowering with the major marks" — these two show the perfection of the essence of the Form Body. The nature of the beauty of the Tathagata's body is its adornment with the major and minor marks. In that regard, he is "graced by the minor marks" because they are the attendants to the major marks. He is "flowering with the major marks" because they serve as the primary ornaments.

"Suitable and harmonious in conduct" shows the perfection of the state. Because he is beautiful in every way he walks, being beautiful in all four postures is the perfection of the state.

"Nothing about him is discordant to behold" shows the perfection of activity. The activity of the Tathagata's body generates great faith through its very essence and generates great faith through its state; thus, there is nothing discordant with sentient beings. <pb n="118"/> Merely by seeing him, one realizes, "This is a Great Being," and generates great faith. This very thing is what is meant by "nothing about him is discordant to behold."

"The delight of those who are devoted with faith; not overwhelmed by wisdom; and not trampled by strengths" — these three phrases show which beings the Blessed One relies upon to perform the welfare of beings. Those beings come before the Tathagata with two types of intentions: either an intention of faith or an intention to overwhelm him. 

The intention of faith is also of two kinds: the intention of wondering "what is he like?" or the intention of great joy. Because both are of the nature of aspiration, they are called "faith." In this way, some develop the intention of wondering what he is like, and being truly exhorted by previous roots of virtue, they go before the Tathagata. Others, having heard of his great virtuous qualities, develop genuine faith, and being exhorted by roots of virtue, they go. Therefore, this shows both those who are neutral and those who have faith. Because he makes them feel joy and develop great faith upon seeing him, the Blessed One is the cause of delight for both those types of devoted people.

The intention to overwhelm is also of two kinds. The intention to overwhelm with wisdom is, for example, like the Truth-Tellers <note>Satyakas</note> who seek debate. The intention to overwhelm with physical strength is, for example, like the forest-dwellers and others who are arrogant regarding their strength. Therefore, this truly shows those who are hostile with these two types of intentions. Because the Blessed One possesses transcendent wisdom and possesses transcendent activity that overwhelms others, he is not overwhelmed by the wisdom of those who wish to overwhelm him, and he is not trampled by their strengths.

"The teacher of all beings; the father of <pb n="119"/> Bodhisattvas; the king of noble individuals; the caravan leader for those traveling to the city of Nirvana" — these four phrases show the Blessed One's performance of whatever activities are necessary for all sentient beings. 

In that regard, "teacher of all beings" means the Blessed One acts as the teacher of activities for all beings without distinction. For example, for some born in the lower realms, by truly showing his light and the body of the Tathagata, he generates faith and establishes them in the higher realms. Among those born in the higher realms, for those who are unsuitable <note>unfit for liberation</note> and who are dominated by the intention to overwhelm in the manner explained before, he establishes them in the path of worldly happiness such as generosity. For those who are suitable and are dominated by the two types of intentions, for those who have not yet generated roots of virtue, he causes them to generate roots of virtue. For those who have generated roots of virtue, he causes their roots of virtue to fully ripen. For those who are fully ripened, he establishes them in the paths of Hearers and so forth according to their respective lineages and brings them to full liberation. Thus, because he accomplishes the activities for those born in the lower and higher realms, and for those who are suitable and unsuitable, he is called the "teacher of all beings."

The distinctions of the stages of that activity are of two kinds: the distinction of the stage of having entered and the distinction of the stage of entering. The distinction of the stage of having entered has two types of lineages, the Buddha-lineage and the Hearer-lineage, for the purpose of accomplishing the arising of a Buddha. Regarding the Buddha-lineage, it says "father of Bodhisattvas." The Blessed One truly entrusts his own perfected qualities to the Bodhisattvas who have attained mastery. Just as a Universal Monarch <term>Chakravartin</term> <gloss>Wheel-Turning King</gloss> <pb n="120"/> truly entrusts the wheel to a son of the Universal Monarch who possesses the marks and becomes the father of those who know, the Blessed One is the "father of those."

Regarding the Hearer-lineage, it says "king of noble individuals." Just as a Universal Monarch becomes the king of his ordinary sons, the Blessed One is like a king to those who have attained realization through the difficult practice of the Hearers.

The distinction of the stage of entering applies to all three lineages while they are in existence. Therefore, regarding that, it says "caravan leader for those traveling to the city of Nirvana." The Blessed One is called a "caravan leader" because he leads those in whom the seed of liberation has not yet arisen into the city of Nirvana, guiding them from one path to another according to their respective lineages.

"Infinite wisdom; inconceivable eloquence; pure speech; melodious voice; a physical presence that one can never look at enough; a peerless body" — these six phrases show the methods by which the Blessed One performs the welfare of beings. Those methods are three. 

In sequence: the first phrase shows the activity of the mind. Three phrases show the activity of speech. Two phrases show the activity of the body. Because the activities of speech and body are the nature of teaching the Dharma and so forth, they are shown as the primary methods for performing the welfare of beings. The activity of the mind is also included as a method for performing the welfare of beings because it instigates all of them. Wisdom is explained here as "mental activity" because it operates together with the mind. Because its objects are infinite, his wisdom is infinite; and possessing that, the Blessed One is called "Infinite Wisdom." The characteristics of the activities of body and speech are held to be the methods for performing the welfare of beings; they are also infinite, and the Tathagata's wisdom engages with them without obstruction. 

The activity of speech shows the specific perfections of the qualities of eloquence and pure melody. In that regard, <pb n="121"/> the specific quality of eloquence is also of two kinds: that based on the letter and that based on the meaning. Regarding eloquence based on the letter, it should be known from the fact that even if he teaches for infinite eons through various distinct letters based on a single word, the Tathagata's eloquence is never exhausted. Regarding eloquence based on the meaning, it should be known from the fact that even when infinite beings individually ask infinite questions over infinite eons, all those questions are answered by the mere utterance of a single word in a single moment. Thus, because he teaches the inconceivable and wondrous Dharma through the specific qualities of eloquence based on letters and meaning, the Blessed One is called "Inconceivable Eloquence."

Because he lacks vocal faults such as speaking lies, and faults of delivery such as speaking in a way that makes hair stand on end, and vocal faults such as having an unpleasant tone, the Blessed One is called "Pure Speech." Because he is pleasing through the quality of his voice, the Blessed One is called "Melodious Voice." The qualities of his speech should be understood from his possessing the five branches or sixty branches of melodic voice.

"A physical presence that one can never look at enough" and "a peerless body" — these two show the specific basis of the body's activity and the specific quality of its essence. In that regard, the specific quality of the basis should be known from "a physical presence that one can never look at enough." Even if one looks at the major and minor limbs of the Blessed One for a very long time, one can never be satiated by the joy of looking, as if seeing them for the first time; thus, it is called "a physical presence that one can never look at enough." The specific quality of its essence should be known from "peerless body." The Blessed One is called "Peerless Body" because he shows colors and behaviors that are harmonious with those to be tamed in various realms, destinies, and birthplaces, and he tames them by teaching the Dharma.

"Unstained by desires; not tainted by forms; unmixed with the formless" <pb n="122"/> — these three phrases show where the Blessed One dwells and how he performs the welfare of beings without attachment. Where does he dwell and perform the welfare of beings? He dwells in the Desire Realm and the Form Realm, because in those realms there is a connection with body and speech. He does not dwell in the Formless Realm; for that very reason, it says "unmixed with the formless." 

In that regard, when the Blessed One performs the welfare of beings in the Desire Realm, because he is not carried away by the desire and passion of the Desire Realm, or by the wrongdoings of the beings belonging to it, he is called "unstained by desires." In the Form Realm as well, when he enters meditative absorption, because his mind is not distracted by the bliss of meditative absorption or by the attraction of being born there through showing the qualities of connection with the beings of that realm, he is "not tainted by forms." "Tainted" means being closely stained; that is, savoring the taste of meditative absorption and savoring the taste of seeing the qualities of birth. Because those are absent, he is "not tainted."

"Completely liberated from the aggregates; not possessing the elements; with sense-bases restrained" — these three phrases show that the Blessed One performs the welfare of beings without attachment to any thing. Those things are the aggregates <term>skandhas</term>, elements <term>dhatus</term>, and sense-bases <term>ayatanas</term>, because external and internal things are of that nature. Those are also the bases of attachment. In that regard, because the aggregates have the nature of repeated birth, by being completely freed from them, the Blessed One is called "completely liberated from the aggregates." Because the elements are the nature of possessing objects through the consciousnesses of the sense-organs, by being free from the afflictions based on them, the Blessed One is "not possessing the elements" <pb n="123"/> in that sense. Because the sense-bases are the gates for the arising of seeing and so forth, by restraining the afflictions based on them, the Blessed One is called "with sense-bases restrained."

"Knots completely severed; liberated from torments; completely liberated from craving; crossed over the flood" — these four phrases show what kind of perfected abandonment the Blessed One possesses when he performs the welfare of beings. Afflictions, in brief, are of two types according to whether one has met with an object or not: those characterized as "knots" and those characterized as "torments." Their gates are also of two types: the gates of craving and the gates of the flood. For those who have not met with an object, they become "knots" through the gate of craving in the form of seeking. For those who have met with an object, because they are carried away like a flood through the gate of prevalent engagement, they become "torments." Because he has abandoned the cravings that are the gates for those respective knots, and the floods that are the gates for those respective torments, the Blessed One is said to have "knots thoroughly severed, liberated from torments, completely liberated from craving, and crossed over the flood."

"Wisdom completely perfected; abiding in the wisdom of the Blessed Buddhas of the past, future, and present; not abiding in Nirvana; abiding at the limit of reality" — these four phrases show what kind of perfected wisdom the Blessed One possesses when he performs the welfare of beings. That wisdom is of three types: omniscient wisdom, non-distinct wisdom, and non-abiding wisdom. <summary>This passage provides a detailed scholastic commentary on the epithets of the Buddha, explaining the perfections of his Form Body, his methods for benefiting beings, his various activities, and his perfected abandonment and wisdom. It utilizes traditional categories like the three realms, the aggregates, and the specific accumulations of merit required to manifest each physical mark of a Buddha.</summary>

"The basis of the treasures of merit" shows the perfection of the distinct causes. The causes for the individual parts of the body are the distinct causes. This should be understood from the teaching on the inexhaustible collection of merit within the teaching on inexhaustible
pages.tail: diligence in the <term>Noble Inexhaustible Intelligence Sūtra</term> <gloss>Arya-Akshayamati-paripriccha</gloss>.

pages.span:
diligence in the <term>Noble Inexhaustible Intelligence Sūtra</term> <gloss>Arya-Akshayamati-paripriccha</gloss>. There it is said that from ten times the mass of merit of all sentient beings, one single hair-pore of the Tathagata is accomplished. From eight times the mass of merit required to accomplish all the hair-pores, one minor mark is accomplished. From a thousand times the mass of merit involved in accomplishing all the minor marks, each major mark is fully accomplished, except for the hair-treasure <note>the urna between the brows</note>, the crown-protrusion <note>ushnisha</note>, and the conch-like dharma-throat. From ten thousand times the mass of merit involved in accomplishing the twenty-nine marks, the hair-treasure is accomplished. From a hundred thousand times the mass of merit involved in accomplishing the hair-treasure, the crown-protrusion is accomplished. From a hundred billion times the mass of merit involved in accomplishing the crown-protrusion, the conch-like dharma-throat of the Tathagata is accomplished. Thus, that Form Body of the Tathagata is the basis of the treasures of merit.

"Graced by the minor marks" and "flowering with the major marks" — these two show the perfection of the essence of the Form Body. The nature of the beauty of the Tathagata's body is its adornment with the major and minor marks. In that regard, he is "graced by the minor marks" because they are the attendants to the major marks. He is "flowering with the major marks" because they serve as the primary ornaments.

"Suitable and harmonious in conduct" shows the perfection of the state. Because he is beautiful in every way he walks, being beautiful in all four postures is the perfection of the state.

"Nothing about him is discordant to behold" shows the perfection of activity. The activity of the Tathagata's body generates great faith through its very essence and generates great faith through its state; thus, there is nothing discordant with sentient beings.

pages.span:
Merely by seeing him, one realizes, "This is a Great Being," and generates great faith. This very thing is what is meant by "nothing about him is discordant to behold."

"The delight of those who are devoted with faith; not overwhelmed by wisdom; and not trampled by strengths" — these three phrases show which beings the Blessed One relies upon to perform the welfare of beings. Those beings come before the Tathagata with two types of intentions: either an intention of faith or an intention to overwhelm him. 

The intention of faith is also of two kinds: the intention of wondering "what is he like?" or the intention of great joy. Because both are of the nature of aspiration, they are called "faith." In this way, some develop the intention of wondering what he is like, and being truly exhorted by previous roots of virtue, they go before the Tathagata. Others, having heard of his great virtuous qualities, develop genuine faith, and being exhorted by roots of virtue, they go. Therefore, this shows both those who are neutral and those who have faith. Because he makes them feel joy and develop great faith upon seeing him, the Blessed One is the cause of delight for both those types of devoted people.

The intention to overwhelm is also of two kinds. The intention to overwhelm with wisdom is, for example, like the Truth-Tellers <note>Satyakas</note> who seek debate. The intention to overwhelm with physical strength is, for example, like the forest-dwellers and others who are arrogant regarding their strength. Therefore, this truly shows those who are hostile with these two types of intentions. Because the Blessed One possesses transcendent wisdom and possesses transcendent activity that overwhelms others, he is not overwhelmed by the wisdom of those who wish to overwhelm him, and he is not trampled by their strengths.

"The teacher of all beings; the father of
pages.tail: Bodhisattvas; the king of noble individuals; the caravan leader for those traveling to the city of Nirvana" — these four phrases show the Blessed One's performance of whatever activities are necessary for all sentient beings.

pages.span:
Bodhisattvas; the king of noble individuals; the caravan leader for those traveling to the city of Nirvana" — these four phrases show the Blessed One's performance of whatever activities are necessary for all sentient beings. 

In that regard, "teacher of all beings" means the Blessed One acts as the teacher of activities for all beings without distinction. For example, for some born in the lower realms, by truly showing his light and the body of the Tathagata, he generates faith and establishes them in the higher realms. Among those born in the higher realms, for those who are unsuitable <note>unfit for liberation</note> and who are dominated by the intention to overwhelm in the manner explained before, he establishes them in the path of worldly happiness such as generosity. For those who are suitable and are dominated by the two types of intentions, for those who have not yet generated roots of virtue, he causes them to generate roots of virtue. For those who have generated roots of virtue, he causes their roots of virtue to fully ripen. For those who are fully ripened, he establishes them in the paths of Hearers and so forth according to their respective lineages and brings them to full liberation. Thus, because he accomplishes the activities for those born in the lower and higher realms, and for those who are suitable and unsuitable, he is called the "teacher of all beings."

The distinctions of the stages of that activity are of two kinds: the distinction of the stage of having entered and the distinction of the stage of entering. The distinction of the stage of having entered has two types of lineages, the Buddha-lineage and the Hearer-lineage, for the purpose of accomplishing the arising of a Buddha. Regarding the Buddha-lineage, it says "father of Bodhisattvas." The Blessed One truly entrusts his own perfected qualities to the Bodhisattvas who have attained mastery. Just as a Universal Monarch <term>Chakravartin</term> <gloss>Wheel-Turning King</gloss>

pages.tail: truly entrusts the wheel to a son of the Universal Monarch who possesses the marks and becomes the father of those who know, the Blessed One is the "father of those."

pages.span:
truly entrusts the wheel to a son of the Universal Monarch who possesses the marks and becomes the father of those who know, the Blessed One is the "father of those."

Regarding the Hearer-lineage, it says "king of noble individuals." Just as a Universal Monarch becomes the king of his ordinary sons, the Blessed One is like a king to those who have attained realization through the difficult practice of the Hearers.

The distinction of the stage of entering applies to all three lineages while they are in existence. Therefore, regarding that, it says "caravan leader for those traveling to the city of Nirvana." The Blessed One is called a "caravan leader" because he leads those in whom the seed of liberation has not yet arisen into the city of Nirvana, guiding them from one path to another according to their respective lineages.

"Infinite wisdom; inconceivable eloquence; pure speech; melodious voice; a physical presence that one can never look at enough; a peerless body" — these six phrases show the methods by which the Blessed One performs the welfare of beings. Those methods are three. 

In sequence: the first phrase shows the activity of the mind. Three phrases show the activity of speech. Two phrases show the activity of the body. Because the activities of speech and body are the nature of teaching the Dharma and so forth, they are shown as the primary methods for performing the welfare of beings. The activity of the mind is also included as a method for performing the welfare of beings because it instigates all of them. Wisdom is explained here as "mental activity" because it operates together with the mind. Because its objects are infinite, his wisdom is infinite; and possessing that, the Blessed One is called "Infinite Wisdom." The characteristics of the activities of body and speech are held to be the methods for performing the welfare of beings; they are also infinite, and the Tathagata's wisdom engages with them without obstruction. 

The activity of speech shows the specific perfections of the qualities of eloquence and pure melody. In that regard,
pages.head: Just as a Universal Monarch <term>Chakravartin</term> <gloss>Wheel-Turning King</gloss>
pages.tail: the specific quality of eloquence is also of two kinds: that based on the letter and that based on the meaning.

pages.span:
the specific quality of eloquence is also of two kinds: that based on the letter and that based on the meaning. Regarding eloquence based on the letter, it should be known from the fact that even if he teaches for infinite eons through various distinct letters based on a single word, the Tathagata's eloquence is never exhausted. Regarding eloquence based on the meaning, it should be known from the fact that even when infinite beings individually ask infinite questions over infinite eons, all those questions are answered by the mere utterance of a single word in a single moment. Thus, because he teaches the inconceivable and wondrous Dharma through the specific qualities of eloquence based on letters and meaning, the Blessed One is called "Inconceivable Eloquence."

Because he lacks vocal faults such as speaking lies, and faults of delivery such as speaking in a way that makes hair stand on end, and vocal faults such as having an unpleasant tone, the Blessed One is called "Pure Speech." Because he is pleasing through the quality of his voice, the Blessed One is called "Melodious Voice." The qualities of his speech should be understood from his possessing the five branches or sixty branches of melodic voice.

"A physical presence that one can never look at enough" and "a peerless body" — these two show the specific basis of the body's activity and the specific quality of its essence. In that regard, the specific quality of the basis should be known from "a physical presence that one can never look at enough." Even if one looks at the major and minor limbs of the Blessed One for a very long time, one can never be satiated by the joy of looking, as if seeing them for the first time; thus, it is called "a physical presence that one can never look at enough." The specific quality of its essence should be known from "peerless body." The Blessed One is called "Peerless Body" because he shows colors and behaviors that are harmonious with those to be tamed in various realms, destinies, and birthplaces, and he tames them by teaching the Dharma.

"Unstained by desires; not tainted by forms; unmixed with the formless"
pages.head: In that regard,
pages.tail: — these three phrases show where the Blessed One dwells and how he performs the welfare of beings without attachment.

pages.span:
— these three phrases show where the Blessed One dwells and how he performs the welfare of beings without attachment. Where does he dwell and perform the welfare of beings? He dwells in the Desire Realm and the Form Realm, because in those realms there is a connection with body and speech. He does not dwell in the Formless Realm; for that very reason, it says "unmixed with the formless." 

In that regard, when the Blessed One performs the welfare of beings in the Desire Realm, because he is not carried away by the desire and passion of the Desire Realm, or by the wrongdoings of the beings belonging to it, he is called "unstained by desires." In the Form Realm as well, when he enters meditative absorption, because his mind is not distracted by the bliss of meditative absorption or by the attraction of being born there through showing the qualities of connection with the beings of that realm, he is "not tainted by forms." "Tainted" means being closely stained; that is, savoring the taste of meditative absorption and savoring the taste of seeing the qualities of birth. Because those are absent, he is "not tainted."

"Completely liberated from the aggregates; not possessing the elements; with sense-bases restrained" — these three phrases show that the Blessed One performs the welfare of beings without attachment to any thing. Those things are the aggregates <term>skandhas</term>, elements <term>dhatus</term>, and sense-bases <term>ayatanas</term>, because external and internal things are of that nature. Those are also the bases of attachment. In that regard, because the aggregates have the nature of repeated birth, by being completely freed from them, the Blessed One is called "completely liberated from the aggregates." Because the elements are the nature of possessing objects through the consciousnesses of the sense-organs, by being free from the afflictions based on them, the Blessed One is "not possessing the elements"
pages.head: "Unstained by desires; not tainted by forms; unmixed with the formless"

pages.span:
in that sense. Because the sense-bases are the gates for the arising of seeing and so forth, by restraining the afflictions based on them, the Blessed One is called "with sense-bases restrained."

"Knots completely severed; liberated from torments; completely liberated from craving; crossed over the flood" — these four phrases show what kind of perfected abandonment the Blessed One possesses when he performs the welfare of beings. Afflictions, in brief, are of two types according to whether one has met with an object or not: those characterized as "knots" and those characterized as "torments." Their gates are also of two types: the gates of craving and the gates of the flood. For those who have not met with an object, they become "knots" through the gate of craving in the form of seeking. For those who have met with an object, because they are carried away like a flood through the gate of prevalent engagement, they become "torments." Because he has abandoned the cravings that are the gates for those respective knots, and the floods that are the gates for those respective torments, the Blessed One is said to have "knots thoroughly severed, liberated from torments, completely liberated from craving, and crossed over the flood."

"Wisdom completely perfected; abiding in the wisdom of the Blessed Buddhas of the past, future, and present; not abiding in Nirvana; abiding at the limit of reality" — these four phrases show what kind of perfected wisdom the Blessed One possesses when he performs the welfare of beings. That wisdom is of three types: omniscient wisdom, non-distinct wisdom, and non-abiding wisdom. In that regard, omniscient wisdom is called "wisdom completely perfected" because it pervades all collections of knowable things and all aspects through wisdom.
